item.description: Subduction recycles surface materials into the mantle and shapes its chemical evolution. Whether continental subduction leaves chalcophile-element imprints in the mantle that differ from those of oceanic subduction remains poorly understood. Here, we show that primitive basaltic magmas from the North China Craton exhibit pronounced copper depletion, silver enrichment, and low copper/silver (200 to 1200), together with continental crust–like trace element patterns and radiogenic-isotope compositions. item.description: Metamorphic proteins challenge the single-sequence-structure-function paradigm by switching between distinct folds that often adopt complementary functions. However, the conformational states sampled along the fold-switching pathway have remained elusive because they are transient and unstable. Using multinuclear chemical exchange saturation transfer and relaxation dispersion NMR, combined with chemical shift–based structure determination and protein engineering, we visualized the atomic resolution structure of an “invisible” state of the metamorphic chemokine lymphotactin. This state is a chimera that integrates the secondary and tertiary structure of one fold with the quaternary assembly of the other. Locking lymphotactin into a single conformation abolishes access to this state, supporting its role as an on-pathway intermediate in metamorphosis. The stabilization of such hybrid intermediates is likely to have facilitated the evolution of fold-switching and represents a powerful strategy for protein design. item.description: Mass-independent isotope fractionation (MIF) of oxygen provides key insights into atmospheric chemistry and the origin of isotopic anomalies in planetary materials. Whether analogous effects can arise in condensed phases or at interfaces remains an open question. These results identify a previously unrecognized class of MIF and provide a quantitative framework for interpreting oxygen isotope signatures in radiation-processed environments, including interstellar grains and early solar system materials. item.title: Effusive sedimentary volcanism experimentally reproduced under Martian-like conditions
item.dc:creator: Ondřej Krýza
Petr Brož
Jacob Adler
Matthew Sylvest

item.description: Abstract Rapid boiling, cooling, and freezing are commonly assumed to rapidly quench metastable liquid eruptions exposed to near-vacuum planetary environments, influencing both sedimentary volcanism on Mars and cryovolcanism on icy worlds. However, how these coupled phase transitions govern eruptive processes remains largely unknown. Here we show experimentally that boiling instead sustains coupled ballistic-effusive mud eruptions under Martian-like pressure conditions (~4.5 mbar). Using an ice-sealed metastable reservoir, we reproduced subsurface-driven eruptions initiated by internally generated boiling-induced overpressure. Eruptions evolved systematically from short-lived ballistic fountains toward episodic effusive emplacement accompanied by coherent mud-flow formation. Ballistic transport redistributed liquid mud around the vent and promoted proximal accumulation that subsequently coalesced into sustained flows despite ongoing cooling and freezing. Numerical modeling further demonstrates that erupted mud would remain largely unfrozen during ballistic transport under Martian gravity conditions. Together, our results show that rapid boiling does not suppress sedimentary volcanism under low-pressure conditions, but instead actively sustains eruptive transport and surface emplacement. These findings provide new constraints on this process on Mars and establish a broader physical framework for metastable liquid eruptions across the Solar System. item.description: Abstract Offshore freshened groundwater (OFG) is a significant yet underexplored component of the global water cycle, and its spatial distribution, particularly its links to past glacial processes, remains poorly constrained. The southeastern North Sea, characterized by extensive tunnel valley networks, provides an ideal setting to test how Pleistocene meltwater shaped offshore groundwater systems. Using newly acquired time-domain controlled-source electromagnetic data integrated with high-resolution seismic reflection surveys, we present a resistivity-based mapping of OFG in this region. The models reveal a laterally continuous OFG body with resistivities of 8–14 Ω·m, extending across multiple stratigraphic units and well beyond individual subglacial landforms. This configuration is best explained by subglacial meltwater flushing of sediment porewaters during Pleistocene glaciations. Subsequent preservation was aided by density contrasts that limit vertical mixing and by fine-grained glaciomarine deposits sealing the system from above. The connection between resistivity anomalies and mapped subglacial landforms shows that the latter can serve as predictive proxies for OFG occurrence. These findings shift the perspective from OFG as isolated anomalies to regionally extensive systems linked to glacial processes, establishing subglacial landforms as a testable screening proxy for locating OFG in formerly glaciated margins worldwide. item.description: Continuous seismic observations and numerical simulations reveal that, over the past decade, fluid migration and microseismic responses at The Geysers geothermal field have been primarily controlled by heterogeneous permeability. Fracture networks directly govern the efficiency of geothermal energy extraction and play a critical role in fluid migration and microearthquake generation. Using deep learning and Markov clustering, we build a high-resolution microseismic catalog covering the past decade for The Geysers geothermal field, California. Our observations reveal distinctive clustering patterns and inferred fracture systems tightly correlated with injection operations. Source mechanism analyses and pore pressure simulations indicate that the inferred connected fracture network provides pathways for rapid and directional pore pressure diffusion, highlighting that heterogeneous permeability controls the localized migration of fluids and the associated microseismic response. Our study highlights the importance of continuous and integrated seismic monitoring for ensuring the sustainability of long-term reservoir development and exploitation. item.description: The global emergence of deep-sea sediments enriched in rare-earth elements and yttrium (REY) after the Late Eocene cooling coincides spatiotemporally with Antarctic bottom water (AABW) expansion, yet the underlying mechanism remains unresolved. Here, we present in situ elemental and neodymium isotopic analyses of apatites extracted from Oligocene-Miocene sediments along the North Pacific AABW pathway. Results show ∼90% of the REY budget resides in inner dentin of fossil teeth. The dentin and coexisting authigenic fluorapatites display similar ε Nd values (∼−5) matching North Pacific seawater, whereas outer dense layer carries a distinct, less-radiogenic ε Nd (∼−10) resembling South Pacific seawater. This isotopic decoupling establishes fossil teeth as dual archives: The outer layer preserves the ε Nd signature of the fish’s living environment, while the inner dentin records its depositional environment. We propose that AABW collects, transports, and sorts fossil teeth along its flow path, ultimately leading to the global occurrence of REY-rich sediments in downstream basins. item.description: Brachiopods appeared early in the Cambrian radiation and represent an important clade for understanding the origin of animal body plans and the evolution of biomineralized structures. item.description: Vegetation greening and abrupt permafrost thaw are reshaping sediment dynamics across the Tibetan Plateau, yet their relative effects on sediment delivery remain poorly quantified. Here we show that retrogressive thaw slumps are disproportionately important sediment sources, with erosion rates two to three orders of magnitude above undisturbed landscapes and source-to-channel connectivity generally exceeding 60%. Combining multi-decadal satellite observations, high-resolution topographic differencing and cold-region hydrological modelling, we quantify the competing effects of thaw-slump sediment supply and greening-induced erosion reduction. During 2000–2022, thaw slumps delivered more than four times as much non-ice sediment to channels as was reduced by greening, compensating for declining glacier-derived sediment and contributing to increased downstream suspended sediment export. Across permafrost regions, approximately 1.2‰ thaw-slump coverage represents an upper-bound threshold above which thaw-slump sediment delivery exceeds greening-induced sediment reduction. These results show that spatially limited abrupt thaw can outweigh widespread vegetation recovery in regulating sediment delivery from warming permafrost landscapes. Abrupt permafrost degradation through retrogressive thaw slumps can increase sediment delivery to Tibetan rivers, outweighing the greening-induced reduction in sediment export, suggests a study combining multi-decadal satellite observations, topographic differencing, and hydrological modelling. item.title: From fragmentation to fault zone architecture as a structural framework for fault weakening
item.dc:creator: Nathalie Casas

item.description: Earthquake nucleation is governed by the evolution of fault zone structure, yet the physical mechanisms linking grain-scale processes to macroscopic weakening remain elusive. Here we use discrete element simulations of quartz-rich gouge in which angular grains fragment dynamically, revealing a robust strain–damage law in which damage accumulates as grains are consumed. Grain size dictates the geometry and timing of localization, while fragmentation enhances compaction and promotes the emergence of a dominant Principal Slip Zone (PSZ). As comminution approaches a saturation state (i.e. minimum grain size), localization can migrate to competing bands, providing a mechanical explanation for overprinted shear fabrics in experiments and natural faults. By linking fragmentation, porosity evolution, and the resulting shear localization, our results provide a local fragmentation state variable for constitutive laws that couple grain-size evolution to fault weakening and the conditions for earthquake nucleation. This study combines simulations and laboratory data to show how grains breaking inside fault gouge reshape fault-zone architecture, focus slip into narrow bands and help faults weaken during deformation. item.description: In Lake Iseo, Italy, human-driven erosion amplified sediment accumulation and preconditioned the delta for catastrophic earthquake-induced collapses and tsunamis, revealing a global mechanism linking human land use to increasing tsunami hazards in lakes. These findings reveal a persistent, human-amplified mechanism of lacustrine tsunami generation and intensity with major implications for hazard assessment. item.description: Cobalt (Co), a strategic critical metal, is significantly sourced from magmatic CuNi sulfide deposits. The Jinchuan deposit, the world's third-largest magmatic CuNi sulfide deposit, provides an ideal setting for studying Co enrichment. This study analyzed ore types (massive, net-textured, and disseminated) from drill core ZK50–3 in Segment II, employing petrography, SEM-EDS, and EPMA to elucidate the distribution, occurrence states, and enrichment mechanisms of Co. Results show that Co primarily resides in pentlandite via isomorphous substitution for Fe2+ and Ni2+, with selective fluid alteration causing anomalous enrichment in secondary magnetite and pyrite. Two key enrichment stages are identified: sulfide liquid segregation (enrichment factor: 39–43) and fractional crystallization of the sulfide melt (enrichment factor: 172–189), with the latter playing a dominant role. This study provides the first quantitative comparison of their relative contributions to Co enrichment. The high-Mg tholeiitic parental magma, relatively enriched in Ni but depleted in Co, was generated by low-degree partial melting of peridotite within a metasomatized, enriched subcontinental lithospheric mantle. During cooling of the sulfide melt, Co preferentially entered the monosulfide solid solution (MSS) and subsequently migrated into pentlandite at 450–550 °C. The presence of pyrite and magnetite with elevated Co concentrations can provide useful exploration clues for CoNi mineralization. In particular, Co-rich hydrothermal magnetite particularly acts as a diagnostic indicator of intensive fluid overprinting. This work elucidates occurrence and enrichment of Co, offering insights for both ore genesis and mineral exploration. item.description: Since the Permian Tarim Large Igneous Province (270–290 Ma) was first recognized, debate has centered on whether to include coeval igneous rocks from the southern Central Asian Orogenic Belt (CAOB). item.description: Two working hypotheses explain the tectonic evolution of the collage of geologic elements comprising the Northern Cordillera of Alaska and Yukon: a long-term eastward subduction scenario and a westward-then-eastward subduction scenario. item.description: Southern Tibet is marked by an ∼15−20-km-thick high-velocity layer in the lowermost crust at depths of 50−70 km, forming a distinct seismic Moho doublet. item.description: This study presents the first Moroccan Cu and Fe isotopic data (δ65Cu and δ56Fe) on (hypogene and) supergene minerals from three polymetallic deposits (Tazalaght, Agoujgal, and Bou Skour) located in the Anti-Atlas Copperbelt. item.description: Marine carbonate archives provide key insights into Earth’s evolving redox state and planetary habitability, preserving carbon-isotope perturbations such as the Lomagundi–Jatuli Event (LJE; ca. 2.22–2.06 Ga), a major global event within the broader interval of the Great Oxidation Event (GOE; ca. 2.45–2.06 Ga). item.dc:creator: Qiang Li

item.description: Carbonate minerals are fundamental components of the sedimentary record, yet their mineralogical and textural diversity cannot be understood from equilibrium thermodynamics or any single crystallization model alone. This review develops an evidence-constrained, pathway-dependent framework that links carbonate nucleation, growth and transformation processes with environmental modulation, structural inheritance, and their expression in the sedimentary record. We distinguish prenucleation solution states from condensed-phase formation and subsequent growth, treating stable prenucleation clusters as a debated model, while integrating ion-by-ion growth, liquid–liquid phase separation, amorphous precursors, particle-mediated growth, and oriented attachment within a common pathway framework. Environmental variables-including supersaturation, temperature, ionic composition, organic matter, EPS, and microbial activity-jointly bias the accessibility, persistence, and transformation of these pathways. Crystallization histories may generate nanoscale structural and compositional features that are selectively inherited by larger-scale carbonate textures; however, pathway–mineral–texture relationships are non-unique, and robust interpretation requires convergent mineralogical, crystallographic, microstructural, geochemical, temporal, and environmental evidence. Applied to the dolomite problem, this framework emphasizes multiple, system-dependent routes by which kinetic barriers to Mg incorporation and Ca–Mg ordering may be overcome, rather than a universal precursor sequence. Together, these elements define an evidence-constrained, non-deterministic pathway–mineral–texture framework that integrates molecular- to nanoscale crystallization processes with environmental modulation, selective structural inheritance, and diagenetic modification, allowing crystallization histories to be evaluated through convergent evidence rather than inferred from mineral identity or texture alone. item.description: The Triassic platform carbonates of the Eastern and Southern Alps host over 500 Pb-Zn deposits collectively known as Alpine-type (AT) Pb-Zn deposits. The AT deposits represent a subclass of Mississippi Valley–Type systems and one of Europe’s largest provinces for base and strategic metals (e.g. Ge, Ga) resources. Despite their importance, the source of metals, timing of mineralization, and mechanism driving fluid flow in the province remain debated. The Raibl deposit (Italy) displays structural and mineralogical features typical of the class, making it an ideal site to investigate controls on Pb-Zn accumulation. This study provides the first, detailed petrographic and compositional characterization of the hydrothermal carbonates associated with the Pb-Zn mineralization at Raibl and present in-situ U-Pb ages on syn- to post-ore carbonate domains alongside new Pb isotopic data on galena from Raibl and other selected AT deposits. Syn-ore carbonates show a distinctive geochemical signature (Fe and Mn enrichment) and constrain the mineralization to a short interval in the Late Triassic (214.0 ± 5.8 Ma to 205.2 ± 3.3 Ma). These constraints support a revised genetic model involving Late Triassic mobilization of oxidized, metal-bearing brines sourced from Permian clastic units (i.e. Val Gardena Sandstone and the Sesto Conglomerate) during early regional extension and strike-slip tectonic. Epigenetic sulphide precipitation at 2–4 km depth resulted from in-situ reduction of these fluids through interaction with organic-rich, Late Triassic lithologies. The proposed model for Raibl aligns with evidence from the world-class Bleiberg deposit but contrasts with smaller mineralized AT systems (e.g. Gorno) that record Middle Triassic, shallow diagenetic mineralization. Overall, the results suggest diachronous fluid flow and metal deposition across the province, emphasizing the role of local structural and geochemical factors in controlling economic accumulation of base metals. item.description: The Nasang Carlin-type Au deposit in southwest China is characterized by abundant late quartz–barite veins that cross-cut earlier sulfide-bearing rocks and locally overlap mineralized zones. Arsenopyrite contains 332–468 ppm Au, compared with 0.01–8.20 ppm in pyrite, and is the most Au-rich sulfide analyzed. item.title: Hot Archean orogens suppressed voluminous S-type granite formation
item.dc:creator: Ming Tang

item.description: S-type granites are far less abundant during much of the Archean than in the Phanerozoic, and this paucity remains puzzling. We propose that the suppression of S-type granite formation at scale may have been an inherent consequence of the hotter Archean crust. A key insight from fossil P-T-t paths in representative orogens is that the onset of melting can trigger exhumation and thereby limit the maximum burial depth of sediments.​ In a hot crust, this maximum burial depth is relatively shallow, because hot geotherms initiate melting at shallow depths due to the pressure dependence of dehydration melting. By contrast, colder geotherms in Phanerozoic orogens effectively suppress melting until higher pressures and temperatures. As a result, Archean sedimentary packages were exhumed too early to undergo extensive decompression and dehydration melting attainable in modern cycles. Phase equilibria modeling shows that the exhuming metasediments in the Archean may only generate melt fractions 1/3 to 1/2 of those in the Phanerozoic. Such low melt productivity in the Archean may have inhibited the formation of large S-type plutons and batholiths. More broadly, these processes may have impeded deep recycling of sediments and, by limiting upward distillation of heat-producing elements, slowed the cooling of the Archean continental crust. item.description: Early Earth’s primordial crustal record has been largely modified and reworked by subsequent tectonic processes, particularly during the onset and evolution of plate tectonics, although remnants of early crustal domains may still be preserved in some terranes. item.description: Sapropelic cryptocrystalline graphite (SCG) occurs in an Early Cambrian rift-platform setting of the South Qinling Orogenic Belt. Nevertheless, the mechanisms of its graphitization and its genetic evolution remain poorly constrained. In this study, we systematically investigated the petrology, geochemistry, and genesis of SCG using X-ray diffraction (XRD), Raman spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and carbon-isotope analysis. The results indicate that SCG and its host rocks occur predominantly in the Cambrian Shuigoukou Formation and Yuejiaping Formation. The associated mineral assemblage comprises quartz, calcite, chlorite, muscovite, phengite, pyrite, and garnet. SCG is characterized by a high degree of graphitization (84–98%) and a high ash content. Graphite crystallites have lateral dimensions of 28–86 nm, stacking heights of 21–30 nm, and interlayer spacings (d 002) of 0.3355–0.3368 nm. Geochemical proxies indicate that the carbonaceous protolith was deposited in a reducing nearshore, shallow-marine setting, with contributions from terrigenous clastic materials and seafloor hydrothermal inputs. Sapropelic organic matter likely represented an important carbonaceous component of the protolith. The δ13CVPDB values of the SCG samples range from −29.84‰ to −19.61‰, consistent with a predominantly biogenic organic-carbon source. Raman geothermometry yields Raman-derived graphitization temperatures of 487.2–513.8 °C. Muscovite and phengite occur mainly as the 2 M1 polytype, with b0 values of 0.9006–0.9047 nm, indicating a medium-pressure metamorphic environment. Combined with regional metamorphic constraints, the estimated pressure–temperature conditions of 0.58–0.79 GPa are consistent with greenschist-facies metamorphism. These results suggest a two-stage evolutionary process involving (1) the accumulation and preservation of organic-rich carbonaceous sediments under reducing marine conditions during the Early Cambrian and (2) subsequent tectono-metamorphic graphitization during regional deformation and metamorphism. Hydrothermal fluid activity, deformation, and mineral matter may have further influenced the graphitization process and contributed to the formation of SCG. item.description: As one of the most pivotal continental blocks in Southeast Asia, the South China Block (SCB) hosts globally significant ore systems and serves as a natural laboratory for studying intracontinental polymetallic mineralization. To constrain its deep lithospheric structure, this study constructed a 3-D lithospheric electrical structure model using magnetotelluric (MT) data from the Qianjiang-Fuzhou Line, a 700-km-long, NW-trending profile with 51 stations. The model reveals pronounced multi-scale heterogeneity in the lithospheric electrical structure, characterized by distinct vertical stratification and lateral discontinuity. A total of eight conductive anomalies (C1-C8) and six resistive anomalies (R1-R6) were identified through the analysis. The Yangtze Block is characterized by high resistivity (>103 Ω·m) as the dominant feature, while the eastern Cathaysia Block contains several prominent crustal-scale conductors (C6, C7, C8) overlain on moderately resistive lithospheric mantle (102-103 Ω·m). In general, the crustal conductors in the eastern SCB support the interpretation of lithospheric dehydration-induced thermal erosion. This process facilitated the ascent of deep-sourced fluids through Late Mesozoic magmatic channels into the upper crust, thereby enhancing crustal conductivity and establishing effective crust-mantle material exchange. Such spatial correspondence between lower-crustal conductors and lithospheric thinning zones further reinforces this mechanism. Meanwhile, our findings align best with a dynamic model tied to the Meso-Cenozoic subduction of the Paleo-Pacific Plate. The tectonic sequence involves initial lithospheric thickening during flat-slab subduction, subsequent large-scale asthenospheric upwelling during slab rollback, and final regional extension and lithospheric thinning driven by slab break-off. This tectonic evolution fostered the formation of a rejuvenated lithosphere and extensive magmatic-minerogenetic systems, while further controlling regional metallogenic distribution through large-scale crust-mantle interactions that remelted both ancient and juvenile crust. In addition, translithospheric fault systems act as conduits for asthenospheric materials and fluid circulation, directly regulating the spatial distribution and metal assemblages of major ore belts to reflect variable shallow responses to deep dynamic processes.
